hints: Look at what has to happen overall, you start with one Br and need two Br atoms on adjacent carbons, so think about what intermediate X must be.
To get from 2-bromopropane to an alkene you need to remove HBr, recall which type of NaOH causes elimination rather than substitution.
Once you have propene, think about which reagent adds two bromine atoms across the double bond in one step.
walkthrough:
**Work out what compound X must be**

Think backwards from the product. 1,2-dibromopropane has Br on C1 and C2.

It is made most easily by adding bromine across a C=C double bond. So X must be the alkene propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$.

**Choose reaction 1: 2-bromopropane to propene**

This is dehydrohalogenation, removal of H and Br to form an alkene. This is an elimination reaction.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{HBr}$$

Elimination of a halogenoalkane needs hot ethanolic NaOH under reflux. Aqueous NaOH would give substitution to an alcohol instead, which is not what we want here.

**Choose reaction 2: propene to 1,2-dibromopropane**

This is electrophilic addition of bromine to the alkene. Both Br atoms add across the double bond at room temperature.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br}$$

$\text{HBr}$ would only add one Br atom and would just give back 2-bromopropane, so $\text{Br}_2(l)$ at room temperature is required.

options.A: Both steps are wrong. Aqueous NaOH gives nucleophilic substitution to propan-2-ol, not elimination to propene. Then HBr addition would not give a dibromo product, as HBr only supplies one Br atom.
options.B: Reaction 2 is correct for an alkene, but reaction 1 is wrong. Aqueous NaOH heated under reflux converts 2-bromopropane to propan-2-ol by substitution, so you would never get propene (compound X) to brominate.
options.C: Reaction 1 is correct, ethanolic NaOH gives propene by elimination. But reaction 2 is wrong. HBr(g) adds H and Br across the double bond to give only a monobromoalkane (in fact 2-bromopropane again), not 1,2-dibromopropane.
options.D: This is correct. Hot ethanolic NaOH eliminates HBr from 2-bromopropane to give propene. Then Br2(l) at room temperature adds across the C=C bond by electrophilic addition to give 1,2-dibromopropane.
